The same gap is what trial.AttractorGuard measures per session: post-rule the recorded top-2 digest makes it observable, because a swap leaves the demoted 'b' second at the SAME margin — so any scored square still read 'b' is one the rule declined to fire on, and min(margin) over correct-'b' squares is the headroom above 0.20 (>=0.20 by construction; warn under +0.05). Squares whose truth is 'b' but read as their runner-up inside the band are only an UPPER BOUND on what the rule took: the pre-rule top-1 is not recorded, so 'the rule demoted it' and 'it was already wrong with b second' are indistinguishable.

Two landmines when writing a serving test that POSTs /estimate with a scripted estimator: (1) if the read comes back as the START position, session.bootstrap_bank fires (§4.6), builds an exemplar bank off the photo and ANSWERS THROUGH the freshly-upgraded ensemble — the response is then not your estimator's output and the test takes ~33s of embedding instead of 0.5s. Use a midgame placement so the start-position gate declines (test_prior_serving.MIDGAME). (2) packages/inference/tests/test_replay.py::test_default_name_tracks_the_model_environment calls replay.default_name(), which REFUSES a dirty working tree — it fails for every agent with uncommitted work in the tree and passes again after the commit; do not chase it as a regression.

FrameRecorder rolls to a new session dir when a frame's seq stops advancing for its board (<=, so a repeated seq counts as a reconnect too). The non-obvious part is the events race: an estimate begun before the roll publishes after it, and seq/frame_seq cannot disambiguate (both sessions start at 0) — only capture_ts can, because sessions are strictly time-ordered. The previous dir's events file is therefore kept open and a line older than the new session's first capture_ts is written there; one level back is enough. Budget: max_bytes stays a whole-run cap, never per dir, or a reconnect resets it and it caps nothing. Readers stay unaware (one session per dir), but replay.find_sessions must remain for pre-roll recordings.

detect_board_quad is a cheap, reliable ONLINE drift monitor on the phone's ingested crops — the opposite of its broadcast-still reputation. Measured over 239 resting frames of the five 08-27 takes: 96% hit rate, ~80-180 ms serial (worst 1.7 s on a miss), and effectively DETERMINISTIC (5 runs on the same frame: median spread 0.00 px, max 0.72 px) despite the _SB_ATTEMPTS docstring's nondeterminism warning. Reason: the client already sends a cropBox crop in which the board fills the frame, which is the easy case. Two gotchas when comparing its quad to an operator/tracker quad: (1) it returns GEOMETRIC TL,TR,BR,BL, so relabel onto the reference quad by nearest-corner over all 8 rotations/reflections — safe, the best-vs-second-best margin measured 9.7x minimum (best <=59 px, second >=533 px), so the a8 labelling is never at risk while drift stays well under half a board; (2) there is a per-session CONSTANT offset of 17-33 px between a finger-dragged operator quad and the detector's playing-surface line (a /detect-originated quad agrees to 4-6 px instead), so ANY absolute distance threshold false-alarms on every hand-framed session — baseline the residual over the first ~3 detections and threshold the change.

Two traps when measuring anything geometric from recordings/*/frames.ndjson. (1) The per-frame 'corners' are in CROP space, not camera space: the camera page cuts cropBox(tracked quad) (CROP_MARGIN 0.1, CROP_HEADROOM 0.3) out of the video and rebases the quad into it via cornersInCrop, so the JPEGs vary in height frame to frame (708-796 px at a fixed 960 width) and the crop FOLLOWS the quad. Displacement of the stamped quad from the session-initial stamped quad is therefore NOT a drift metric — a real camera move largely cancels. Compare the stamped quad against detect_board_quad on the SAME frame, and normalise by square width (mean quad edge / 8), not by frame diagonal: a read breaks when the grid slips a square, and QUAD_VERIFY_SHIFT=0.03 of the diagonal happens to be ~0.47 square here. (2) seq is NOT globally monotonic — recordings/20260827-175539 (take 4) holds a 48-frame FALSE START and then restarts seq at 0 on reconnect, so keying frames by seq silently drops one stream and baselining on frames[0] invents an 84 px step. Split on the last seq restart before measuring.

Framing-drift re-detection (packages/viewer/ui camera state.ts): the best-vs-second-best CORNER CORRESPONDENCE margin is not a scale-free safety check, so guard ordering decides what the operator is told. For a pure translation d of a board with side S, the runner-up ordering costs ~S+d, so margin = (S+d)/d and only falls under 4x once d > S/3 -- i.e. past ADOPT_MAX_SHIFT_SQUARES (2 squares) already. If the margin is checked FIRST, every genuine reposition comes back 'ambiguous' and the >2-square 'suspect' branch that surfaces the nag is unreachable (this is exactly how the first implementation failed its own test). Correct order: use the margin to gate the two things that would corrupt state -- contributing to the baseline R0, and ADOPTING a quad (a bad match is how a8 moves) -- and classify 'too far to be drift' from the baselined shift alone. Second, normalise the shift by the TRACKED quad's square width, not the detected one: the tracked grid is the one actually cutting squares, and a spurious undersized detection would otherwise divide a moderate disagreement into a huge one.

The per-session baseline R0 in the camera page's drift re-detection (median of the first 3 detected-minus-tracked corner offsets) is a PIXEL-SPACE offset describing one particular corner convention, so it must be reset on every deliberate re-framing, not just at session start: a handle drag (the operator's corner line moves), a successful /detect (the convention becomes the detector's, ~0 offset), a board switch, and any frame-size change (the pixels themselves are re-based). Keeping a stale R0 makes the very next reading look permanently shifted by the whole convention delta (17-33 px measured, ~0.3 square) and can fire a false adoption that yanks the operator's own corners back. It is deliberately NOT reset after an adoption -- the correction is expressed as detected-minus-R0, so the convention is unchanged. The reset hook cannot be anchorTracker(), which adoption also calls.

packages/viewer/ui: the /camera page hands the camera and the quad to exactly ONE activity at a time (the Activity union), so every request that claims the slot must be bounded or the whole page wedges silently -- drag, detect, calibrate and both auto flows are all gated on activity.kind === 'idle' and none of them shows a reason when they are disabled. fetch has no default timeout, so api.ts detect() now carries AbortSignal.timeout(DETECT_TIMEOUT_MS = 15s) and requestJson translates a TimeoutError into status 0 / 'the node did not answer in time' (distinct from the unreachable-viewer message). Bound it at the api.ts endpoint rather than per caller: all three detect callers claim the same slot. Second rule for any background self-check: a plain interval with no failure budget hammers a dead endpoint for the whole session -- mirror shouldAutoDetect's consecutive-miss backoff plus give-up, and reset the budget on any answer at all (not just a useful one) and on any deliberate reframe.

Driving the recorder's post-roll late-event race through the REAL gateway is deterministic, no sleeps: FrameIngest runs the estimator in asyncio.to_thread, so a fake estimator that blocks on a threading.Event parks exactly one read in its worker thread while the event loop keeps acking; the /ingest handler records (and therefore rolls) INLINE before it acks, so a returned ack is proof the roll already landed on disk; releasing the gate then publishes an event whose capture_ts belongs to the already-closed directory. Two constraints make or break it: (1) send both sessions over ONE websocket — WebSocketDisconnect makes the handler 'await ingest_.drain(*boards)', which would finish the parked read before the roll and dissolve the race; (2) wait on an 'entered' Event before sending session B's frame, or the latest-wins maxsize=1 inbox replaces the un-picked-up frame and nothing is ever in flight. Mutation-checked: forcing FrameRecorder._belongs_to_previous to False fails only the race test, forcing _starts_a_new_session to False fails all four.

Driving the /camera page's 10 s / 20-40-80 s timers in Playwright: page.clock.install() leaves the clock RUNNING in real time (only pauseAt stops it), fakes performance.now AND AbortSignal.timeout — so the page's 15 s detect bound is drivable — and fastForward(ms) fires each due timer ONCE at the FAR END of the jump. That last detail is the trap: the frame loop's next tick then reads a performance.now() that moved by the whole window while video.currentTime did not move at all, which is exactly what the camera-stall watchdog catches (2 s -> play(), 6 s -> REOPEN THE CAMERA, losing the framing mid-test). So cross the clock in steps of ~1.5 s with ~120 ms of REAL time between them for the camera to deliver a frame and reset changedAt. Second rule: advance to an ABSOLUTE performance.now() mark, never by a duration — the clock is still running, so every expect() between two jumps spends the very budget being measured, and 'advance 19 s' really advances 19 s plus however long the assertions took. Third: the drawn-canvas camera (tests/helpers/camera.ts) is required for anything clock-driven, because its rAF draw loop is what keeps currentTime advancing and its static board is what keeps the tracker locked — Chromium's --use-fake-device pattern makes the tracker report lost, and a 6 s sustained loss fires an auto-detect that resets the whole drift baseline.

Two production bugs the /camera e2e cascade caught that unit tests could not, both from a type too wide to mean anything. (1) shouldAutoCalibrate's grid was 'readonly (readonly string[])[]' and looksLikeStartOccupancy compared cells against 'empty' (protocol.CLASSES's vocabulary), but the page hands it board.grid from $lib/board/fen, where an empty square is ''. Both are string, so it type-checked, every square read as OCCUPIED, and the zero-tap calibration was unreachable in the browser for the whole life of the feature while its unit test (which built grids out of 'empty') passed. Fixed by taking an Occupancy = boolean[][] and doing the one conversion at the caller. Rule: when two layers spell the same domain differently, the shared predicate must take neither vocabulary. (2) camera.spec.ts's calibrateIntoRotateWarning had been red since 0b2857c (23 commits) because a calibration reply carrying label_rotation is now ABSORBED (setFraming + labelsNeedCheck = false), so it no longer raises the 'rotate labels' warning. The only thing that still does is an automatic re-detection that MOVED an existing framing — reachable in a test by seeding localStorage's saved crop off the board (seedFraming) and stubbing /detect onto it.

Estimation scheduling (schedule.py, measured 2026-08-27 over the four 08-27 takes, 25 replays, scratch/experiments/move_trigger/): reading at BURST END + a 3 s keepalive floor instead of every frame is a 12-16x read/GPU cut for a pooled -0.9pp prior per-square, and on three of four takes the boards a policy selects are INSIDE the 95% band of a random subsample of every-frame's own scored boards. That null result is structural, not a weak policy: trial.py already drops guard_seqs=12 frames after every truth boundary, i.e. the mid-move window, so the 'chaos frames' a burst-end policy exists to skip were never in the scored population and skipping them CANNOT show up as a score. Burst-end reads really are calmer (median stability of read frames 0.94-0.98 -> 0.99, fraction >0.85 from ~60% to 72-93%) — these takes' errors are just persistent piece-type confusions (q->k, p->b), not motion blur. So justify scheduling on GPU budget and display stability, never on accuracy. Cost side: settle latency 3.5 s -> 5.5 s median, and burst_end_reads=1 can never settle anything (BoardStabilizer wants SETTLE_MIN_READS=2 spanning SETTLE_SECONDS=2.5, and one read per move is not a quorum) — burst_end_reads=3 at spacing_s=1.3 spans 2.6 s and is the only setting where a burst end settles on its own evidence. Two gotchas that will bite the next sweep: (1) the 12-30x saving is inflated by history — three takes were recorded at a flat 8.3 fps because the motion meter was broken; on take 5 (the only one through the FIXED adaptive forwarder) the arriving stream is already 82% in-burst and the same policy buys only 5x, with prior perfect dropping 31.2->20.0, at the low edge of chance. Expect ~5x live, and apply the policy to the ingest INBOX (prefer_frame already keeps the sharper contender) rather than the raw arrival stream. (2) read sparsity does NOT fix the settled lock-in, it perturbs it: the control take's every-frame settled stream is wrong on 253/253 boards (all q->k on d8, adopted first read and never displaced, settled 96.1% BELOW its own prior 97.2%) and sparse policies get 2-3/7 segments instead of 0/7, while the hard take goes 10/10 -> 6-7/10. stabilize.py's adopt-first-wholesale rule is the defect at every read rate.

Replay's frame-policy seam is per-frame DETERMINISTIC across policies: over 4 takes x 5 sparse policies, every read of a given frame_seq produced the byte-identical raw AND prior board as the every-frame replay (919/919 events). The raw/prior streams of any scheduling policy are therefore a pure SUBSET of one every-frame run - so a new policy's raw/prior score can be computed offline from a single every-frame replay's events.ndjson plus the policy's should_estimate() over the index, and only the stateful "settled" stream needs an actual GPU replay. An every-frame replay costs ~1.3 GPU-s per frame (GTX 1650, cascade+bank ensemble); a sparse one is proportional. Also verified: --restamp-stability changes the schedule and NOTHING else - restamped vs unrestamped every-frame on the same stack gave 337/337 events byte-identical outside the "stability" field. Two traps when using pre-existing replay dirs as comparators: (a) baseline-3452334 and bdemotion-fe8a7bb were built by a CascadeEstimator (the session bank failed to load in that session) while the same env today builds an EnsembleEstimator - ALWAYS read manifest.replay.estimator before diffing two replay dirs, the env block alone looks identical; (b) trial.py's guard_seqs window is counted in SEQS, so at take 5's ~2 fps arrival rate the same guard=12 excludes ~6 s per boundary versus ~1.4 s at 8.3 fps, and it removes a much larger FRACTION of a sparse policy's reads than of every-frame's.

Replay/serve from a worktree or any non-repo cwd silently drops the bank: DEFAULT_DINOV2_ONNX is cwd-relative (models/dinov2_small.onnx, embed.py) and _estimator_from_bank's failure path is a silent 'pass' (server.py ~314) — the stack degrades to cascade-only with no warning; the only tell is the estimator config line in reports. Export BR_DINOV2_ONNX absolute (like BR_MODEL) whenever cwd != repo root, and always check the report's estimator line before comparing runs. Two replay sets are only comparable if that line matches.

The settled stream's real defect was never a 'tiebreak': BoardStabilizer settles per square with no constraint on the board those squares COMPOSE, so two squares can settle on halves of two mutually exclusive readings. Measured on the 08-27 control take at every frame: d8 settled 'k' from one reading of the k/q swap while e8 settled 'k' from the other, and 233/337 published settled boards carried TWO BLACK KINGS - a board no repaired read ever claimed and no truth segment can ever equal, which is exactly what 'settled 96.1% below its own prior 97.2%, 0/253 perfect, never settles a segment' was made of. Fix that shipped: a commit may not raise the board's hard-constraint excess (prior.violation, oriented=False) above what the settled board already carries; when it would, the squares the SAME read disagrees on that already hold >=SETTLE_MIN_READS consistent reads are dragged into the commit, best-evidence-first, until it does not. The drag terminates because its fixed point is the read itself, which the prior already repaired. Result over 4 takes x 6 policies: 0 impossible settled boards (was up to 69% of a run), control every-frame settled 96.1->97.2% with perfect 0->28.1% and 4/7 segments settling, pooled settled-perfect 37.7->40.5%, and the settled board changed LESS often (437->425 changes). Do NOT reach for the obvious alternatives first: letting a persistent minority accumulate votes (windowed majority, or long-horizon attrition over a contested episode) was scored on all 24 runs and lost on every pooled axis (perfect 37.7 -> 33-36%, more flicker) - because the unbroken-run rule is a quality filter, and any rule that settles MORE also settles noise.

Settled-stream semantics can be designed with ZERO GPU: the prior stream is fixed by the estimator, so any recorded replay dir (recordings/*/replays/mt-*) can be re-settled with a candidate BoardStabilizer over its recorded prior placements and re-scored through trial.py's own _score_stream. 24 runs re-score in ~2 s, and the sanity gate is exact - the current stabilizer must reproduce the recorded settled row of every report.json to the digit (it does). Use it before spending an hour of GPU on a replay sweep. Two things that harness immediately settles: (1) the two convicting data sources are NOT the same failure - on the 08-13 take the prior itself reads the d8/e8 swap on 671/748 events (90%), so settled holding it for 748 straight events is the debounce faithfully reporting what the reads say, and settled (96.9%) BEATS prior (95.4%) there; only the 08-27 control take's every-frame run is real stabilizer evidence. (2) 'settled per-square >= prior per-square' is not a fair acceptance bar on short takes: decomposing the control take's settled errors against the PREVIOUS truth segment shows 231 of them are pure settle lag (the board is 2.5 s behind while trial.py's guard only excludes 12 frames ~ 1.25 s after a boundary), so a 35 s take with a move every 5 s pays that on ~1/3 of its scored events no matter how good the debounce is. Compare the NON-lag error count instead: on that take the fix takes it from 400 to 226 against the prior's 447.

Live read scheduling (schedule.py + ingest.py, shipped 2026-08-27): the seam that makes ONE policy serve both the offline replay and the live gateway is OBSERVE-AT-SUBMIT / DECIDE-AT-DRAIN. FramePolicy is observe(capture_ts, stability) + due(capture_ts, stability), with should_estimate(FrameEntry) = observe-then-due for replay (byte-identical to the old single-method version). Live, FrameIngest.submit() observes EVERY arriving frame (burst end is only visible from the whole run; the maxsize=1 latest-wins inbox would hide most of it) and the worker calls due() on whichever frame it actually picked — which is what lets prefer_frame's sharper contender be the frame a burst-end read is spent on (the sweep's take-5 weakness). due() is NOT a pure query: answering True consumes the read, so it must be asked exactly once per frame the caller can estimate, and AFTER the Uncalibrated check (a frame nothing could read must not spend the board's read budget). Types: policies take two floats, never a header object — a recorded FrameEntry.header is a dict but a wire Frame.header is a METHOD, so ingest._schedule_signal is an explicit adapter through schedule.stability_of (the one coercion boundary: null/NaN/missing stability -> 1.0, D3 'at rest', because NaN loses every comparison and would slip through the hysteresis' calm branch and declare a move complete mid-hand).

A capture-time read floor (D3) has FIVE ways to be switched off, and four of them are in the policy rather than the sensor — found by adversarial review of schedule.BurstTriggered before it went live, each now a test in test_schedule.py/test_ingest_schedule.py. (1) Owed burst-end reads spilling into the NEXT burst: while owed the interval is the tight spacing_s, so two moves closer together than the run is long make the leftovers fire mid-hand at 1.3 s and hand the debounce a quorum that disagrees by construction (verified: stabilities [0.97]*20+[0.3]*10+[0.97]*10+[0.3]*25+[0.97]*30 @8.3fps read seqs 47 and 58 inside the second move). Entering a burst must CANCEL owed. (2) keepalive_s=inf passes a bare '>0' and means never; keepalive_s=nan passes it too and INVERTS the limit to every-frame, because every comparison against NaN is False. Require math.isfinite AND >0. (3) spacing_s > keepalive_s silently overrides the floor (when-still k=3 spacing=10 -> 10 s gaps under a claimed 3 s floor). (4) A backwards clock: re-anchoring by CLEARING last_read_ts makes the surprising frame due, so a monotonically decreasing capture_ts reads 50/50 frames — re-anchor to ts instead (elapsed clamps to 0) and phrase the check as 'elapsed >= interval' rather than 'elapsed < interval' so a NaN capture_ts also answers 'not yet' instead of 'read everything'. (5) A FROZEN capture_ts cannot be fixed inside a capture-time policy at all without killing replay determinism — it belongs at the ingest layer: the worker carries a monotonic-clock backstop at BACKSTOP_SLACK=2x keepalive_s (2x, not 1x, so growing ingest latency does not trip it and frames_backstopped stays a real diagnostic of a broken edge clock). Also: %g in a policy's canonical name is a correctness bug, not cosmetics — it renders burst_end_reads=1000000 as '1e+06' which parse_policy then refuses, and rounds floats to 6 significant digits so two different policies share one name and one replay directory. Format ints as ints and floats with repr (trim a bare '.0').

BR_SCHEDULE product default lives in cli.cmd_serve (os.environ.setdefault), NOT in server.create_app — deliberately, following the BR_RECORD_DIR precedent: a real server always schedules, while create_app() with no env reads every frame, so the existing gateway tests that stream N frames and assert N estimates keep meaning what they meant. Both live entry points (compose.yaml and make dev) run "board-reader-inference serve", so the CLI default reaches production and nothing else constructs the app. Consequences for testing: (a) a test that wants the shipped behaviour must monkeypatch.setenv("BR_SCHEDULE", DEFAULT_POLICY_SPEC) — including the pipe e2e in tests/test_end_to_end.py; (b) a test of cmd_serve itself must swap os.environ for a private dict (monkeypatch.setattr(os, "environ", dict(os.environ))), because monkeypatch cannot restore a key the code under test sets; (c) counting estimates through a real WS /ingest socket is only deterministic for SPARSE policies — the latest-wins inbox drops frames under a fast socket even with a stub estimator, so every-frame must be asserted as estimated+dropped+unscheduled==N, never estimated==N. DEFAULT_POLICY_SPEC is "burst-end:burst_end_reads=3" because keepalive_s=3.0 and spacing_s=1.3 are already the dataclass defaults and a spec states only what was asked for.

A per-square coherence rule (commit only if the board's hard-constraint excess does not rise) STARVES without a deadline, and the starving case is not exotic: settled holds 'k' on d8, every single read says 'q', but committing d8 alone composes two black queens while the e8 partner that would relieve it flickers below the quorum and is never draggable — 200 reads / 260 s and the square never lands. Bound it: a ripe square blocked for STALE_WINDOWS=2 windows waives the quorum on its partners and drags them in evidence order until the excess is satisfied, which caps staleness at ~3x settle_seconds (one window to ripen, two to time out). Two details that matter. (1) Keep the outer guard '_excess(read) <= held_excess' before entering the escape: it makes the loop's terminal state (the whole contested set = the read) provably safe, so the escape can never fall through, AND it keeps 'an impossible read is never adopted' true no matter how long the read persists. (2) Take the escape SURGICALLY — same drag with quorum waived, stopping as soon as the excess clears — not the whole contested set: on the one real run where starvation bit (hard take, burst-end k=3 n=2, 0.5 reads/s) wholesale took 9 squares for -0.71pp, surgical took 7 for -0.56pp. Cost over 24 recorded runs: exactly 1 run's settled stream changes at all, pooled per-square -0.016pp, perfect-board rate identical. Cheap insurance against an unbounded-staleness bug.

A seeded 'property test' over random boards can be completely vacuous and look thorough. The first version here drew each square independently from all 13 classes at 0.4 s spacing against a 2.5 s settle window: 580 _commit calls, ZERO commits — nothing ever ripened, so a stabilizer with the coherence check deleted passed it. Three things make such a test real, and all three are cheap: (1) generate a DRIFTING board (start from a real placement, perturb a few squares per read) out of a SMALL alphabet, at a spacing that lets runs span the window; (2) assert the mutant fails — keep a subclass with the pre-fix logic in the test file and assert the same helper returns True for it; (3) assert PATH COVERAGE, not just that something happened — spy on the guarded method and assert the set of code paths taken equals the expected set, so the test fails loudly when a generator change stops exercising one. Sweeping two settle windows (1.0 s and 1.5 s) was needed to hit all five paths here. Same trap for order-dependent code: both drag-order tests had exactly one eligible candidate, so reversing the sort or dropping it for row-major passed everything — an order test needs TWO candidates that are eligible at the same instant and would give different boards.

A post-hoc re-rank rule's safety margin is a property of the takes it was measured on, not of the model: the b-demotion shipped on a 0.210 min-correct-margin gap ('0 broken'); the 08-28 trial closed it to 0.208 and an A/B replay (same take, same bank, ATTRACTOR_MARGIN 0.20 vs 0.0) showed the rule now trades eaten correct bishops (b->P x9) against prevented empty->b hallucinations (x8) — net +4 settled, a wash elsewhere. The eval-session attractor guard caught it; trust the guard and settle such questions with replay-vs-replay, never by reading the post-rule digest.

A bank-backed baseline must pin its own bank snapshot (e.g. data/eval/bank-baseline-20260828.npz): the live exemplars_session.npz mutates by design — the 08-28 trial's auto-calibrate grew it 768->1024 mid-take, and 1024 is the maturity threshold that flips the blend 50/50->30/70, changing the stack itself, not just the data. A baseline quoted against the live bank is stale the moment anyone calibrates.

truth.json for a recorded take can be authored by monotone alignment of the expected placement sequence against events.ndjson (best-match with a small look-ahead window, boundary = first frame_seq matching the next position) — but from_seq must be strictly increasing, so plies with no event between them (burst-end scheduling reads only at move end) collapse into one segment carrying the later placement; guard_seqs=3 absorbs the noisy mid-move reads at each boundary.

Masked-crop retraining (occlusion masking baked into the cropcache) matched run_e's synthetic holdout exactly (0.898) and beat it +3.2pp on chesscog_transfer scored UNMASKED — training-time masking regularizes beyond its serving domain. Gate any deploy on the replay takes, not the holdout.

Never overlap a cropcache build with torch training on this box: the resident dataset plus a second copy-heavy job exhausted 31GiB and hard-froze the machine (2026-08-28). Run heavy jobs one at a time under systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryHigh=12G -p MemoryMax=16G with num_workers<=4.

runpodctl v2 live gotchas (each cost a paid pod to learn): (1) CLI-created pods publish NO ports by default — always pass --ports 22/tcp or 'pod create --wait' hangs forever and resolve_ssh finds nothing ('pod get' says: pod does not publish 22/tcp); (2) --wait prefixes 'waiting for ssh on pod <id>' text lines to its JSON output — json.load the whole stream fails, parse from the first '{' line; (3) network volumes forbid chown — rsync -a (implies -og) exits 23 and set -e turns that cosmetic miss into a dead pod; use -rlptD; (4) network volumes exist only in some DCs (EU-SE-1 is NOT one) — the create error lists the valid DCs; (5) staging needs no pod at all: the S3-compatible API (bucket=volume id, s3api-<dc>.runpod.io, separate S3 key) uploads straight to the volume — vital because EU-RO-1 routinely has zero CPU instances; (6) community GPU stock churns minute-to-minute: poll tiers cheapest-first and treat 'no instances available' as retryable, everything post-create as not.

Member-level model gains do not compose with a bank-dominant cascade: run_g/run_h beat their baselines by +4pp on unseen real photos yet LOST every replay take deployed (masked or unmasked serving) — E6's d8 q<->k win was the BANK's nearest-exemplar lookup unlatching under masked embedder inputs, not a classifier effect. Gate deployed configurations on take replays, never on member evals. Bonus defect found: settled coherence resolves 'two kings' by demoting the CORRECT one, doubling a single q->k into a symmetric swap on every event.

The prior decoder's two-king repair is ALREADY evidence-based (prior._kings_flip demotes the lowest p(king), shipped faaa4ed 2026-08-13) — do not re-open it as 'it demotes by flip cost'. Re-measured 2026-08-28 on the shipped cascade+bank (run_e/run_f, bank-baseline-20260828, BR_CROP_MASK=gray) over all four gates.sh takes: on 20260813-193308 the rule splits 17 d8 / 17 e8 because the evidence genuinely crosses — the bank-locked FALSE king d8 reads k at a stable 0.33-0.41 with a fat 0.17-0.24 margin while the TRUE king e8 ranges 0.20-0.45 with margins down to 0.003. Three alternatives scored across all four takes: 'margin' (the pre-faaa4ed rule, and the actual MAP answer under square independence) collapses 08-13 to 2/31 settled; 'max-margin' and 'neg-entropy' buy 08-13 (27/31, 22/31 vs shipped 22/31) by demoting the MORE confident king — anti-MAP, winning only because this take's bank lock makes the wrong king the confident one — and they cost 20260827-175539 5/12 -> 2/12 settled perfect (0.9609 -> 0.9440 per square) and 20260828-111421 0.9266 -> 0.9096. Shipped 'prob' is Pareto-best across the four. Ceiling check: an oracle that always demotes d8 gives prior 21/31 and settled 29/31, vs shipped 15/31 and 22/31 — so the stabilizer already recovers most of the coin flip and only ~7 settled boards are reachable by ANY per-frame tie-break. The residual lever is recognition on d8 or a temporal identity prior, never another per-frame rule. Method note: decode() and BoardStabilizer are pure, so rule search needs ONE GPU replay — monkeypatch board_reader_inference.ingest.decode to capture every square_dist, then offline recompute prior+settled into a recording-shaped dir and score with trial.run(Recording.open(dir)). Also: replay rows are not interchangeable evidence — the '31/31 settled swap, e8 demoted' figure comes from the e7-masked row (run_g/run_h, a REJECTED candidate), while the shipped e6f-gray row is 9/31.

Rebuilding the session exemplar bank offline from data/uploads calibrate sidecars is a supported operation: `board-reader-inference rebuild-bank --uploads data/uploads --mask {gray,blur,none} -o <npz>` (board_reader_inference.rebuild). It reuses calibrate_from's exact machinery — crop_squares_photo at FRESH_BANK_GEOMETRY (hr=0.3 sp=0.15), build_exemplars with augment=True/T=0.1/backbone dinov2 — so a rebuild differs from a live-grown bank only in masking and corpus membership. Two gotchas: (1) crop_squares_photo(mask=None) means READ BR_CROP_MASK, not 'off', so an unmasked rebuild must force the env (rebuild.crop_mask context manager) or it silently inherits the serving default; (2) ExemplarClassifier.__init__ re-normalises on ingest, so a saved bank does not round-trip bit-identically through load — assert allclose, never array_equal. Augmentation makes one calibrate photo 256 exemplars, so the 54-board corpus is 13824 rows (APPEND_BANK_CAP is 20000, so it still fits the live ceiling).

Masked-bank rebuild, three-way curated eval (run_e+run_f cascade, BR_CROP_MASK=gray serving, 5 curated boards / 320 squares, 2026-08-28): bank-baseline (1024 exemplars, live-grown, UNMASKED) 305/320 95.3%; bank-rebuilt-unmasked (13824, uploads corpus) 308/320 96.2%; bank-masked (13824, same corpus, gray-masked exemplars) 309/320 96.6%. So most of the win is the CORPUS (+3), masking on top of it is +1 — masking exemplars changed 72% of the 13824 rows (max |delta| 0.21) yet moved one square. Perfect boards stayed 0/5 in all three. Side effect worth knowing before touching any confidence threshold: the 13.5x bigger bank drops mean board confidence 0.59 -> 0.51-0.53 (more exemplars raise every class's max-cosine, flattening the softmax), and per-board residuals REORDER (baseline's f7 Q->B / h8 k->B partly go away, d8 q->k appears on boards that were clean) — bank writes are not monotone, exactly as STATUS warns. Do not read a curated delta as a deployment verdict: gate on take replays.

Bank rebuild from data/uploads MUST run the label guard and exclude rectified warps — measured 2026-08-28 on the 54-upload corpus: only 31 survive. 10 fail session.verify_labels TODAY (5x at 1/32 piece agreement, 1x at 7/32, and 4x the 2026-08-27 portrait-phone incident that report '30/32 once turned 90deg'), and 13 are already-rectified 384x384 warps whose corners ARE the image border. The warps are doubly wrong for a photo bank: at uniform camera depth nothing occludes anything, so occlusion masking is provably a no-op on them (0/64 crops changed), meaning they dilute exactly the gray-vs-none contrast a masked rebuild exists to measure. Nothing on disk marks a sidecar as audited, so an unguarded rebuild silently embeds colour-swapped exemplars. Second trap: the guard probes through crop_squares_photo too, so it must be pinned to unmasked (rebuild.crop_mask(None)) or the accepted corpus becomes a function of --mask and the masked/unmasked pair stops being a controlled comparison.

Guarded masked-bank rebuild, three-way curated eval (run_e+run_f, BR_CROP_MASK=gray serving, 5 curated boards / 320 squares, 2026-08-28): bank-baseline (1024 exemplars, live-grown, UNMASKED) 305/320 95.3%; bank-rebuilt-unmasked (7936, 31 guarded uploads) 307/320 95.9%; bank-masked (7936, SAME 31 uploads, gray-masked) 308/320 96.2%. Corpus +2, masking +1; perfect boards 0/5 throughout; masking changed 7536/7936 rows. Note vs the earlier UNGUARDED rebuild (13824 rows, 54 uploads, 308/309): the polluted version scored ~1 square higher AND collapsed mean board confidence 0.59 -> 0.51, while the guarded 7936-row bank holds confidence at 0.57-0.63, i.e. baseline-like. So a bigger bank is not a better bank: the rejected/rectified rows were buying a per-square point by flattening every softmax. Judge a rebuilt bank on confidence calibration as well as per-square, and gate deployment on take replays, never on this curated set (the bank's own calibrate photos are not held out from it).

Bank experiments must control for session membership before any other variable is interpretable: the live bank's value is auto-calibrate exemplars grown from the deployed sessions' own frames (pixels only in recordings/, never in data/uploads), so any upload-corpus rebuild silently swaps 'session-adapted' for 'corpus-clean' and loses the takes while winning curated (08-29: 35->22 perfect despite curated 305->308). Corollary: curated is doubly not a deployment verdict for banks.

Full-data training (true 663k epochs, run_i) lifts the synthetic holdout (+2.9pp) while DROPPING real-photo transfer (chesscog 0.860->0.828): more synthetic data per epoch overfits the style mix. Select members on chesscog_transfer, never the holdout; the steps_per_epoch cap was accidentally protective.

Hand-authoring truth labels for board photos: resolve which detected corner is a8 WITHOUT the model. autocalib.resolve_rotation reads model predictions, so using it to orient a truth label makes the label partly a model output. Two model-free checks suffice and are cheap: (1) back-rank luminance — pick the quarter-turn whose top two rows are darkest (black men on ranks 7-8); only one of four rotations puts black on top, and the margin is huge (27-62 grey levels measured on the 08-31 batch). (2) chirality — a rotation cannot mirror, but a wrongly-wound quad can, so check the a1-is-a-dark-square invariant on the EMPTY middle ranks (a3 dark < b3 light, a4 light > b4 dark); pieces occlude the back ranks so sample ranks 3-4, not 1-8. Verify both by eye on a rectified contact sheet before writing labels.

data/eval/ground_truth.json is BOTH the eval label set and the source corpus for the shipped exemplar bank (tools/build_exemplar_bank.py reads it directly). So a photo landed there is bank material and can never be a held-out eval board. To keep a board genuinely held out, write it as a *.label.json sidecar instead: the eval loader (labels.load_labels) rglobs both shapes under data/eval, but the bank builder only ever opens ground_truth.json. A .label.json needs its photo adjacent in the same directory (symlinks are fine) and corners as an 'x0,y0,...,x3,y3' STRING, not a nested list — that is parse_corners' contract, and it differs from ground_truth.json's corners_a8_h8_h1_a1 list-of-pairs.

A per-frame decode-rule change can reach the oracle on one dataset and score ZERO on another: the 08-31 two-kings reopen's p(K)-p(Q) won the stills sweep (+5 squares, no curated loss) then collapsed 08-13 from 22/31 to 0/31 settled in the replay gate — the queen-mass polarity inverts between datasets and a lambda sweep showed no safe amount. A stills win is evidence to RUN the 4-take replay gate, never to ship; and a rule that needs the 'right' dataset is a fitted constant.

replay.CONFIG_ENV omits BR_CROP_MASK, so a masked and an unmasked replay of the same take share a config_digest (measured: e6-control vs e6-gray on 181802, both cc530662, scoring 0.9139 vs 0.9121). Until fixed, never trust a stored replay dir's digest to identify the masking config — re-run the baseline instead. Also: events.ndjson carries only the top-2 evidence digest (4dp), which cannot feed the 13-class decoder — capture full square_dist at experiment time or the experiment's inputs are unrecoverable (the 08-28 two-kings captures were lost this way).

A calibrate bank write can raise EVERY per-square metric (raw/prior/settled, all four takes, stills, ECE -0.116) while dropping deployment-relevant settled-perfect boards 35->25 — the 08-31 candidate bank killed the fresh style's decoded Q->K (4->0) but pulled the 08-13 true king's p(k) down ~0.05 uniformly, flipping the tie-break 17/34->26/34 wrong. Gate bank writes on the 4-take settled-PERFECT rows, never per-square or stills; and expect cross-style writes to contaminate the king/queen margin on the styles NOT just calibrated.

DINOv3 as a frozen bank embedder is a NO-GO: cross-style ceiling ~80->83% (n.s.), and the central-column pooling +9 is DINOv2-SPECIFIC — under DINOv3 central lands 12 squares behind CLS and gives back the piece-id gain. Central pooling's durable property is occupancy (.994+), an occupancy-head asset only. DINOv3 CLS is banked as a mildly better fine-tune init (first frozen encoder to cut piece-id errors instead of trading vs occupancy); exports in models/dinov3_vits16*.onnx. Verify normalization from the model's own preprocessor_config before any backbone A/B — DINOv3 happens to match DINOv2's ImageNet stats.

The 4-take replay gate silently becomes a MEMORIZATION READOUT for any candidate trained on its sessions: run_j0 (trained on hand-truth crops from 4 gate takes) scored +20 settled-perfect boards while every uncontaminated signal (chesscog, curated-through-cascade, synthetic holdout) was flat or negative — measured 100% of gate-scored boards within 5 frames (<1s) of a trained image. gates.sh needs a scoring-side contamination check (training style sources vs gate sessions); until it exists, never quote a gate row for a candidate whose training touched those recordings.

RunPod stock listings are near-worthless: 'Low' is the highest status the API shows and coexists with 100% create failure. Probe capacity by CREATE (pod create -o json, parse id, delete instantly, ~1c per hit); when dry, run a 60s retry loop grepping for 'no longer any instances' (retry ONLY on that error so the loop can never retry-spend) — stock churns in minutes, the 08-31 run landed on round 3 after hours of slow-poll failures.

ChessQ Lite V6 (BR_CHESSQ, chessq.ChessQEstimator) replay gate 2026-11-24: settled perfect 35->71/109 vs tkr-shipped, but settled TRAILS prior on 3 of 4 takes (75 prior vs 71 settled): the BoardStabilizer (2.5 s, 2 reads) under burst-end (~0.4 reads/s) lags a reader whose raw reads are already right; 8 of 15 settled-wrong boards are the previous position verbatim. Prior repair is a no-op for ChessQ (raw==prior on every take). Its raw errors are mid-move frames: arm-covered squares read EMPTY at p>=0.96, never uncertain, so any faster settle needs a hand gate. Also: the release has TWO outputs (logits, direction) - request 'logits' by name, trained._onnx_logits_fn's output[0] convention is not safe for it.

Truth-file repair recipe (2026-11-24, fixed 181802's early stop and 111421's merged two-move segments): sweep ChessQ Lite V6 over EVERY frame of the suspect range to get placement runs (long stable runs = real positions, 1-frame runs = hand transitions), check each boundary by eye on a contact sheet of board crops, then build the placements by pushing SAN moves with python-chess from the last trusted segment, so the result is legal by construction. A segment that changes two pieces of different colours is a merged-move bug. Replays symlink truth.json to the take's own file, so eval-session on the replay dir rescores without re-reading.

One read path (Phase B, 2026-11-24): create_app takes a Recognizer, but FrameIngest and replay.replay take a FrameRead = Callable[[Frame], PositionEvent], built by recognizer.frame_reader(recognizer). The split is deliberate: a Recognizer only sees pixels, so a test fake that must answer per seq/board_id (scripted reads, delays, failures) is a plain FrameRead, while the gateway and replay.run always wrap the real recognizer. build_from_env() returns the Recognizer itself (ChessQRecognizer, or StubRecognizer with .fallback set when BR_CHESSQ is unset/missing — that is what /healthz reports).

ChessQ reads 0/14 core.sim renders perfectly, so any test that needs a recognizer reading REAL pixels uses tests/_sim_recognizer.SimRecognizer: a per-square template match against render_board templates at the same square size — exact even through a JPEG round trip (42/42 placements x sizes 24/32/48). It is importable as 'from _sim_recognizer import SimRecognizer' from tests/ (pytest prepend import mode puts tests/ on sys.path); inference package tests cannot import it, they use StubRecognizer or a FrameRead fake. To make a recognizer fake single out ONE frame (e.g. gate its read), compare the image it is handed with decode_jpeg(frame.encode()[1]) — exactly what /ingest decodes.

The replay-gate invariant for a refactor is stronger than gate_table's totals: diff each take's replays/<name>/events.ndjson against replays/cq-v6 line by line on (frame_seq, placement, prior, settled) — Phase B held all three deletion steps to identical lines (and |dconfidence|=0). make gate takes ~75 s even on a loaded box (the int8 ChessQ runs ~2 reads/s on CUDA; the burst-end policy reads 133 frames over the 4 takes). Delete intermediate replay dirs afterwards; keep cq-v6 and tkr-shipped (tkr-shipped can only be rescored by eval-session now, never re-replayed).

In a checkout shared with another live session, never pre-stage: a 'git rm' or 'git add' sits in the shared index, and the other session's bare 'git commit' takes it. That happened on 2026-11-24: 332a32f, a docs commit, swept in Phase B's staged deletions of session.py, autocalib.py, rebuild.py and the bank tools. Delete with plain rm, then commit with 'git commit -F msg -- <paths>'. A pathspec commit records worktree deletions of tracked files and ignores the rest of the index. A brand-new file still needs 'git add', so run it in the same command as the commit.

ChessQ V6 fp32 ONNX export (tools/chessq_export, torch 2.8 TorchScript exporter, opset 17) is BYTE-reproducible under the locked env: re-exports give the same SHA-256, so the committed export descriptor pins exact bytes. Gotcha: no-op dtype casts (image.to(float32), logits.float()) still emit ONNX Cast nodes, so dropping them changes the SHA (b9ebec59cafc7d706f7403baff93642daa3a0daa61796b8e231fa2caba659f2b with casts vs f4ea7628c8fb9edda47b12c866fa0fb3129095fab9242912c1acb205e162264f without) though the math is identical — keep the wrapper's forward exactly as exported. Parity check that isolates the export: feed Predictor.prepare_image's tensor to both the package (CPU fp32) and ORT; max |dlogit| ~3e-5. Hardware choice: fp32 205 ms on GTX 1650 CUDA vs int8 600+ (MatMulInteger has no CUDA kernels); on CPU int8 663 ms vs fp32 986 ms — so one release, two files, chosen per entry point (tests/test_deploy_parity.py pins GPU<=>fp32).

Settle/schedule tuning without the GPU: the recognizer is stateless, so read EVERY frame of a take once (cache (seq, square_dist)), then run replay.replay() with a memoized FrameRead (event_from_dist(frame, cache[seq])) per schedule (~1 s/take, byte-identical events.ndjson to a real replay - verified on all 4 gate takes) and re-run BoardStabilizer over that replay's prior placements per settle config (ms). Finding: the settle window only matters relative to the burst-end run's span ((burst_end_reads-1)*spacing_s); a window longer than the run waits for the 3 s keepalive. With one read per move (plain burst-end, what the gate used to replay though serve never ran it) no window helps. Shipped 1.0 s/2 reads + burst_end_reads=3,spacing_s=0.6: gate settled 84/101 -> 104/119, median move-to-settle 4.3 -> 3.0 s, 0 hand leaks. stale_windows changed nothing anywhere in the grid. Held-out takes 163352/170333/172736 must be replayed with --restamp-stability (broken meter) or every schedule collapses to keepalive; their truths look incomplete (d3, ...Bc5, Nc3, ...Qe7 never in truth but read for stretches).
